# Technical Details of Sliced-Wasserstein Distance-Based Data Selection

## 1. Problem Formulation

The method compares an empirical distribution of a dataset against itself with individual samples removed. Formally, given a dataset $\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}\{\mathbf{z}_i\}$ with N samples in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the approach constructs an empirical distribution $\hat{\mathbb{P}}_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{\mathbf{z}_i}(\mathbf{z})$ where $\delta_{\mathbf{z}_i}$ assigns probability mass to each sample. A leave-one-out variant $\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_i}$ removes sample i. The core concept evaluates "transportation cost of individual data samples with respect to the rest of the dataset" by measuring distributional differences using sliced-Wasserstein distance.

## 2. Sliced-Wasserstein Distance for Filtering

The sliced-Wasserstein distance projects high-dimensional distributions onto one-dimensional representations along randomly sampled directions. Its finite approximation is:

$$SW_{\|\cdot\|,t}(\mathbb{U},\mathbb{V})\approx\left(\frac{1}{L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}W_{\|\cdot\|,t}(\mathfrak{R}\mathbb{U}(\cdot,\bm{\theta}_l),\mathfrak{R}\mathbb{V}(\cdot,\bm{\theta}_l))^t\right)^{1/t}$$

where $\mathfrak{R}$ denotes Radon transforms (linear projections) along directions $\bm{\theta}_l$ uniformly distributed on the unit sphere.

## 3. Voting Mechanism

The SWAD (Sliced-Wasserstein Anomaly Detection) algorithm employs a voting system:

- For each sample i, n random samples are selected from the dataset minus i
- Each vote compares $SW(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_i}, \hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_j})$ against threshold $\epsilon > 0$
- A vote is positive if distance $\geq \epsilon$
- Sample i is labeled an outlier if positive vote proportion $\geq$ threshold p

The voting indicator function is: $\Psi_{\|\cdot\|,t}(i,j,\epsilon)=\text{1}(SW_{\|\cdot\|,t}(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_i}, \hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_j})\geq\epsilon)$

## 4. Two Scalability Approximations

**Smart Split-SWAD (sSWAD):**
Clusters the dataset into K clusters, then randomly splits each into S reduced-cardinality representations. Each split processes concurrently with adjusted thresholds: $\epsilon_s = \frac{|\mathcal{D}_s|}{|\mathcal{D}|}\epsilon$ and $n_s = \frac{|\mathcal{D}_s|}{|\mathcal{D}|}n$. Final outlier set approximates: $\mathcal{O}\approx\bigcup_{s=1}^{S}\mathcal{O}_s$

**Fast Euclidian Approximation (FEAD):**
Replaces expensive sliced-Wasserstein computation with norm distances. Proposition 1 establishes bounds:

$$\frac{\|\mathbf{z}_k-\mathbf{z}_l\|}{(N-1)}\leq W_{\|\cdot\|,t}(\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_k},\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_l})\leq\frac{\|\mathbf{z}_k-\mathbf{z}_l\|}{\sqrt[t]{(N-1)}}$$

FEAD replaces distance comparisons with Euclidian distances, becoming "extremely fast" while maintaining theoretical connection to Wasserstein distance.

## 5. Stated Limitations

- Method "does not scale well with large datasets"
- Cannot distinguish local from global outliers; "observation that we can generate three filtering scenarios...we filter only...statistical outliers...we only keep...closest to the barycenter"
- "Not a jack-of-all-trades" 
- "Biggest limitations...lack of proper theoretical guarantees for out-of-sample model predictive performance"
- FEAD may be "less accurate...when t≠1"

## 6. Individual Data Point Scoring

Points are scored through a voting mechanism based on pairwise distance comparisons. A point receives a confidence score reflecting "proportion of positive votes" out of n comparisons. Higher proportions indicate stronger outlier likelihood. The authors note ability to "measure the algorithm's confidence in its labelling" through voting percentages, enabling conservative data selection by adjusting threshold p.

## 7. Barycenters and Consensus

The work mentions adjusting $\epsilon$ values such that the filter "only keep[s] the samples closest to the barycenter of the majority group." However, no explicit barycenter computation or consensus mechanism is described. The barycentre appears implicitly through the voting mechanism's tendency to retain central samples.

## 8. Experimental Setup and Results

**Data Selection Experiment:**
- Six UCI regression datasets (wine, forest, solar, energy, concrete, stock)
- 10% test split; 30% validation from remaining 90%
- Gaussian noise (variance 0.05) corrupts training/validation data
- Shallow convex neural networks with max 25 hidden neurons trained via ℓ₁-loss
- Tree-structured Parzen estimator for hyperparameter optimization, 100 trials per method
- Results shown as normalized mean absolute error (MAE), normalized to [0,1] per dataset

**FEAD Performance:** Achieved lowest average normalized errors (0.3786) versus sSWAD (0.5300), Isolation Forest (0.5419), Local Outlier Factor (0.7312), and no filtering (0.5081)

**LCPR Dataset Benchmark:**
- 197 anonymous customers across three Montréal substations over two years
- Winter peak forecasting using Gaussian processes with rolling horizon
- Testing period: 2023-12-15 to 2024-04-15
- Results show MAE ranging 17.9–41.2 kWh across substations

## 9. Mathematical Formulations

**Order-t Wasserstein Distance:**
$$W_{\|\cdot\|,t}(\mathbb{U},\mathbb{V})=\left(\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{J}(\mathbb{U},\mathbb{V})}\int_{\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}}\|\mathbf{z}_1-\mathbf{z}_2\|^t d\pi(\mathbf{z}_1,\mathbf{z}_2)\right)^{1/t}$$

**SWAD Outlier Set Definition:**
$$\mathcal{O}=\{\mathbf{z}_i\in\mathcal{D}|p\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\mathbf{z}_j\sim\hat{\mathbb{P}}_{N-1}^{-\mathbf{z}_i}}\Psi_{\|\cdot\|,t}(i,j,\epsilon)\}$$

**FEAD Approximation:**
$$\mathcal{O}\approx\{\mathbf{z}_i|p\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_j\text{1}\left(\frac{\|\mathbf{z}_i-\mathbf{z}_j\|_2}{\sqrt[t]{N-1}}\geq\eta\right)\}$$

**Lemma 1 (t=1 equivalence):** For t=1, the single-sample transportation plan equals the optimal Wasserstein plan, proven using triangle inequality.

**Theorem 1:** Establishes that sliced-Wasserstein bounds regular Wasserstein distance with constants dependent on dimension d and order t.

## Key Research Areas

**Demonstration Selection for In-Context Learning:**

The selection of few-shot examples (exemplars/demonstration samples) is essential for constructing effective prompts under context-length budget constraints, and this task can be formulated as a top-m best arms identification problem. CASE (Challenger Arm Sampling for Exemplar selection) is a novel sample-efficient selective exploration strategy that maintains a shortlist of "challenger" arms and reduces sample complexity and LLM evaluations.

**Reinforcement Learning Approaches:**

The Relevance-Diversity Enhanced Selection (RDES) leverages reinforcement learning frameworks to optimize the selection of diverse reference demonstrations for in-context learning tasks, employing Q-learning and PPO-based variants to dynamically identify demonstrations that maximize both diversity and relevance.

**Optimal Transport in Few-Shot Learning:**

PLOT-TAL is a framework that leverages Optimal Transport (OT) to find a globally optimal alignment between prompt ensembles and video temporal features. This method establishes state-of-the-art results on few-shot benchmarks of THUMOS'14 and EPIC-Kitchens without requiring complex meta-learning.

**Many-Shot In-Context Learning:**

Recent approaches combine demonstrations selected based on similarity to test samples with larger sets of demonstrations selected using k-means clustering on centroids derived from test sample representations.

## Full Abstract

"Dataset Distillation (DD) aims to generate a compact synthetic dataset that enables models to achieve performance comparable to training on the full large dataset, significantly reducing computational costs."

The researchers propose WMDD (Wasserstein Metric-based Dataset Distillation), which leverages optimal transport theory for improved distribution matching.

## Wasserstein Barycenter Approach

The method uses Wasserstein barycenters in a specific way:

1. **Feature Extraction**: They compute the Wasserstein barycenter of features derived from a pretrained classifier

2. **Distribution Capture**: This barycenter represents essential characteristics of the original data distribution

3. **Synthetic Data Optimization**: Synthetic data is optimized to align with this barycenter in feature space

4. **Variance Preservation**: Per-class BatchNorm statistics are leveraged to maintain intra-class variations

## Key Results

The approach maintains efficiency while achieving state-of-the-art performance across high-resolution datasets. The paper was accepted to ICCV 2025, with code and a project page publicly available.

The core innovation centers on using optimal transport theory's barycenter concept to bridge the synthetic and real data distributions more effectively than prior methods.

The paper presents "a new unsupervised anomaly (outlier) detection (AD) method using the sliced-Wasserstein metric." The authors emphasize that this filtering technique is valuable for machine learning operations pipelines in critical sectors like energy, as it enables conservative data selection. Additionally, they introduce "the first dataset showcasing localized critical peak rebate demand response in a northern climate" and demonstrate their approach on synthetic datasets and standard anomaly detection benchmarks.

The core contribution centers on applying the sliced-Wasserstein metric—a computational variant of optimal transport theory—to identify anomalous data points without requiring labeled training examples. This unsupervised approach is particularly suited for production environments where data quality assurance is essential before deploying models in sensitive applications.

- Benchmark evaluation across multiple dataset types

### Core Methodology

The framework formulates data selection for task-specific finetuning as an optimization problem based on optimal transport for distribution alignment, with a regularization term that encourages diversity.

In the optimization objective, optimal transport is used to measure the discrepancy between the distribution assigned to the candidates and the target distribution, encouraging the alignment between them.

The framework supports distribution alignment in any metric space that supports efficient nearest-neighbor search, including model-agnostic semantic embedding and model-specific features such as gradients.

The framework adds a regularizer to encourage the diversity of the selected data and incorporates kernel density estimation into the regularizer to reduce the negative effects of near-duplicates among the candidate data.

### Implementation

The framework proposes efficient algorithms including KNN-Uniform and KNN-KDE to assign probability mass to the candidates, with each algorithm taking query examples and candidates as input and outputting the probability assigned to each candidate.

## Distributional Process Reward Models: Calibrated Prediction of Future Rewards via Conditional Optimal Transport

The paper addresses the problem that Process Reward Models (PRMs) used in inference-time scaling are often poorly calibrated and overestimate success probabilities. The authors propose the first use of conditional optimal transport for calibrating PRMs, modifying conditional OT map learning to estimate a monotonic conditional quantile function over success probabilities estimated by the PRM, conditioned on PRM hidden states.

The evaluation was conducted on mathematical reasoning benchmarks spanning moderate-difficulty problems (MATH-500) and harder out-of-distribution problems (AIME), with results showing that for PRMs with reliable ranking signals, the method substantially improves calibration over both uncalibrated PRMs and quantile regression.

On downstream Best-of-N IAS performance, the method generally improves over uncalibrated PRMs, establishing conditional optimal transport as another principled and practical approach to PRM calibration, offering structural guarantees and flexible uncertainty estimation.

# FDMat: Feature Distribution Matching for Coreset Selection

## Abstract Summary

The paper addresses computational costs in deep learning by proposing FDMat, a method that tackles an understudied problem: "the skewed distribution between the coreset and the entire dataset." The authors establish that when a selected coreset's feature distribution closely mirrors the full dataset, the resulting model exhibits superior generalization, especially under aggressive pruning scenarios.

## Method Overview

Rather than employing gradient-based selection techniques, FDMat takes a distribution-centric approach. The core innovation involves reformulating coreset selection as "an optimal transport problem from the coreset to the entire dataset in feature embedding spaces." This mathematical framework enables the algorithm to identify samples whose feature distributions are most representative of the complete dataset.

## Key Advantages

The method demonstrates robustness by naturally filtering outliers and problematic samples. As noted in the abstract, it shows "strong robustness due to the removal of samples far from the distribution, especially for the entire dataset containing noisy and class-imbalanced samples." This characteristic makes it particularly valuable for real-world datasets with quality issues.

The experimental validation across multiple benchmarks confirms that FDMat outperforms existing coreset selection methods while maintaining computational efficiency.

# TSDS Data Selection Method Overview

## Full Abstract

"Finetuning foundation models for specific tasks is an emerging paradigm in modern machine learning. The efficacy of task-specific finetuning largely depends on the selection of appropriate training data. We present TSDS (Task-Specific Data Selection), a framework to select data for task-specific model finetuning, guided by a small but representative set of examples from the target task. To do so, we formulate data selection for task-specific finetuning as an optimization problem with a distribution alignment loss based on optimal transport to capture the discrepancy between the selected data and the target distribution. In addition, we add a regularizer to encourage the diversity of the selected data and incorporate kernel density estimation into the regularizer to reduce the negative effects of near-duplicates among the candidate data. We connect our optimization problem to nearest neighbor search and design efficient algorithms to compute the optimal solution based on approximate nearest neighbor search techniques. We evaluate our method on data selection for both continued pretraining and instruction tuning of language models. We show that instruction tuning using data selected by our method with a 1% selection ratio often outperforms using the full dataset and beats the baseline selection methods by 1.5 points in F1 score on average."

## Optimal Transport Application

The TSDS method employs optimal transport through a **distribution alignment loss**. This loss quantifies the divergence separating the chosen training examples from the target task distribution. By formulating the selection challenge as an optimization problem centered on this OT-based loss function, the authors can systematically identify which data points best match the desired distribution characteristics while maintaining diversity through an additional regularizer incorporating kernel density estimation.

## Detailed Findings on Pallage 2025 (arXiv 2504.12918) and Related OT-based Data Selection Work

### 1. WHAT IS THE PALLAGE METHOD?

**Paper:** "Sliced-Wasserstein Distance-based Data Selection" by Julien Pallage and Antoine Lesage-Landry (Polytechnique Montreal), April 2025. This is an extended version of their earlier paper [arXiv:2410.21712](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21712).

**Core idea:** An unsupervised anomaly detection method called SWAD (Sliced-Wasserstein Anomaly Detection) that uses the sliced-Wasserstein (SW) distance to identify and remove outlier data points before training ML models.

**Algorithm in detail:**

- Given a dataset D of N samples in R^d, construct an empirical distribution P_N = (1/N) sum of Dirac deltas at each point.
- For each candidate point z_i, construct a **leave-one-out** distribution P_{N-1}^{-z_i} (the empirical distribution with z_i removed).
- To decide if z_i is an outlier: draw n random reference points z_j from the dataset (excluding z_i), compute the SW distance between P_{N-1}^{-z_i} and P_{N-1}^{-z_j} for each, and check if that distance exceeds a threshold epsilon.
- Each comparison constitutes a **vote**: if SW(P_{N-1}^{-z_i}, P_{N-1}^{-z_j}) >= epsilon, it is a positive (outlier) vote.
- A point z_i is labeled an outlier if the proportion of positive votes >= threshold p.
- The voting percentage serves as a **confidence score** for the outlier label.

**The sliced-Wasserstein distance itself** works by projecting high-dimensional distributions onto random 1D directions (via Radon transforms), computing the 1D Wasserstein distance on each projection (which is just sorting + L1/Lp), then averaging over L random directions. This avoids the cubic cost of full OT.

**Two scalability approximations:**

1. **Smart Split-SWAD (sSWAD):** Clusters the dataset into K clusters, randomly splits each into S reduced subsets, runs SWAD on each subset concurrently with proportionally adjusted thresholds (epsilon_s and n_s scaled by subset/dataset ratio), and unions the outlier sets.
2. **FEAD (Fast Euclidean Approximation Distance):** Exploits a proven bound that for single-sample perturbations, the Wasserstein distance between leave-one-out distributions is bounded by ||z_k - z_l|| / (N-1) <= W(...) <= ||z_k - z_l|| / (N-1)^{1/t}. This lets them replace the expensive SW computation with simple Euclidean distance comparisons, making it "extremely fast."

**Application domain:** Primarily power systems / energy forecasting. They introduce a dataset for localized critical peak rebate demand response in northern climates (Montreal).

---

### 2. HOW DOES IT RELATE TO USING OT FOR DEMONSTRATION QUALITY SCORING?

The connection is **indirect but conceptually meaningful**:

**What Pallage does:** Uses OT (specifically SW distance) to measure how much the overall data distribution changes when a single point is removed. Points whose removal causes large distributional shifts are outliers; points whose removal causes negligible shifts are "typical" and retained. The voting mechanism across multiple reference removals provides a confidence-calibrated quality score per data point.

**Relation to demonstration quality scoring:** If you were scoring demonstrations for, say, in-context learning or imitation learning, the Pallage approach would amount to asking: "Is this demonstration consistent with the rest of the demonstration set?" A high-quality demonstration would have low transportation cost (removing it barely changes the distribution), while an anomalous or low-quality demonstration would have high cost. This is a **distributional typicality** measure, not a **task-performance** measure.

**Key distinction:** Pallage's method scores quality purely based on statistical typicality within the dataset -- it has no notion of a target task, a reward signal, or downstream performance. It filters out statistical outliers, not functionally poor demonstrations. This is fundamentally different from methods like TSDS (NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2410.11303](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11303)) which use OT to match the selected subset's distribution to a **target task distribution**.

---

### 3. WHAT ARE ITS LIMITATIONS?

The paper explicitly acknowledges several:

1. **Scalability:** The base SWAD algorithm does not scale well to large datasets (the pairwise leave-one-out SW computations are expensive). The approximations (sSWAD, FEAD) mitigate but don't fully solve this.
2. **Cannot distinguish local from global outliers:** The method identifies points far from the overall distribution. Depending on the epsilon threshold, it either filters only extreme statistical outliers or aggressively keeps only points closest to the barycenter. There is no middle ground for detecting local structure violations.
3. **No theoretical guarantees for downstream model performance:** The biggest admitted limitation. Filtering outliers from training data does not come with any formal guarantees that the resulting trained model will perform better. The connection to downstream predictive quality is purely empirical.
4. **FEAD approximation accuracy degrades for t != 1:** The Euclidean approximation is tightest for Wasserstein-1; for higher-order Wasserstein, the bounds loosen.
5. **Unsupervised / task-agnostic:** It has no mechanism to incorporate task-specific objectives. It filters based on distributional typicality alone, which may discard rare but valuable data points (e.g., rare edge cases that are crucial for generalization).
6. **Threshold sensitivity:** The method requires setting epsilon (distance threshold) and p (voting threshold), which are hyperparameters without clear automatic selection criteria.

---

### 4. HOW DIFFERENT IS IT FROM WASSERSTEIN BARYCENTERS FOR CONSENSUS-BASED QUALITY SCORING?

These are substantially different approaches:

| Aspect | Pallage SWAD | Wasserstein Barycenter Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Core computation** | Pairwise SW distances between leave-one-out distributions | Computing the barycenter (Frechet mean in Wasserstein space) of a set of distributions |
| **What it measures** | How much removing a point perturbs the overall distribution | How far each point/distribution is from the consensus center |
| **Scoring mechanism** | Voting over random pairwise comparisons | Distance from individual point to the computed barycenter |
| **Computational cost** | O(n^2) pairwise comparisons (before approximations) | Solving a multi-marginal OT problem (also expensive, but different structure) |
| **Consensus notion** | Implicit -- points retained are those that don't perturb the distribution, so they implicitly define the "consensus" | Explicit -- the barycenter IS the consensus, and quality = proximity to it |
| **Strengths** | No need to compute a barycenter; voting provides confidence calibration | Principled geometric center in distribution space; natural for aggregating multiple sources |
| **Limitations** | Indirect quality measure; no explicit reference distribution | Expensive to compute exactly; sensitive to outliers in the input distributions |

**The WMDD paper** (Liu et al., ICCV 2025, [arXiv:2311.18531](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.18531)) is actually the closest example of Wasserstein barycenters applied to data quality/selection: it computes the Wasserstein barycenter of features from a pretrained classifier to capture "essential characteristics" of the data distribution, then optimizes synthetic data to match this barycenter. This is dataset distillation rather than filtering, but it demonstrates how barycenters serve as an explicit consensus representation.

**Key conceptual difference:** Pallage's approach is *relative* (each point scored relative to random subsets via voting), while barycenter approaches are *absolute* (each point scored by its distance to a fixed geometric center). The barycenter approach provides a more principled "consensus quality" metric but at higher computational cost and with the requirement to actually solve the barycenter problem.

---

### 5. RELATED WORK: OT FOR DATA FILTERING/SELECTION (2025-2026)

Several significant related works:

- **TSDS** (Liu et al., NeurIPS 2024, [arXiv:2410.11303](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11303)): Formulates task-specific data selection for LLM finetuning as an OT problem -- uses OT-based distribution alignment loss to match selected subset to target task distribution, plus a KDE-based diversity regularizer. Achieves strong results with just 1% selection ratio.

- **FDMat** (AAAI 2024, [paper](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28771)): Frames coreset selection as an OT problem in feature embedding space -- selects subsets whose feature distribution is closest (in OT sense) to the full dataset. Shows natural robustness to noisy/imbalanced data.

- **WMDD** (Liu et al., ICCV 2025, [arXiv:2311.18531](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.18531)): Uses Wasserstein barycenters for dataset distillation -- computes feature-space barycenters to capture essential distribution characteristics, then generates synthetic data aligned to these barycenters.

- **Distributional Process Reward Models** (Ma et al., 2025, [arXiv:2605.06785](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06785)): Uses conditional OT for calibrating process reward models in LLM reasoning -- not data selection per se, but uses OT to score/calibrate quality of reasoning steps.

- **DRoP** (Distributionally Robust Pruning, [arXiv:2404.05579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.05579)): Uses distributionally robust optimization (which has OT connections via Wasserstein balls) for data pruning.

- **FAST** (CVPR 2025): Frequency-domain distribution matching for coreset selection, using Characteristic Function Distance as an alternative to OT for distributional matching.

- **Zero-Shot Offline Imitation Learning via OT** ([arXiv:2410.08751](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.08751)): Uses OT for matching demonstration distributions in imitation learning settings.

The overall trend is a clear movement from using OT merely as a loss function (e.g., in generative models) toward using it as a **principled framework for data selection, filtering, and quality assessment** -- with methods spanning unsupervised outlier detection (Pallage), task-aware subset selection (TSDS), distribution-matching coreset selection (FDMat), and synthetic data generation (WMDD).
